Game Explorer

Every game, White and Black alike - not just the ones with a deviation. Click "View" to step through the actual game move by move on a board; if there was a deviation, it opens right there with your move and the book's move shown as arrows. Losses with a real deviation are listed first.

Study Queue

Turns every place you've left the book into a flashcard: shows the position right where you deviated and asks what your repertoire actually plays there. Needs synced games matched against an active repertoire to have anything to show - same data as Game Explorer and Study Priority.

Load Your Own Games

Runs entirely in your browser - nothing is uploaded anywhere. Once your games are loaded, head to the Results tab to see deviations, study priority, and auto-detected structures & plans - and check the Repertoire tab to make sure it's actually comparing against what you play.

1a. Sync directly from Chess.com or Lichess

Pulls your recent games straight from the platform - no export/upload needed. Note: this needs the page to be actually hosted somewhere (like GitHub Pages) with real internet access; opening the raw file directly from your computer often blocks this kind of request.

(months back for Chess.com, or number of recent games for Lichess)

1b. Or upload a PGN file directly - OTB, Lichess, Chess.com, anywhere

Playing over the board, or your games just aren't on Chess.com/Lichess? Export a PGN from wherever you keep your games (tournament software, a TD's export, a Lichess study, anything standard) and drop it in here - same analysis either way. Handles annotated files with variations and evaluation marks fine, not just flat exports.

Time-based is more predictable; depth-based is more consistent in strength but can vary a lot in speed position to position.

Manage Your Repertoire

What you're actually supposed to be playing - this is what your games on the Sync tab get checked against. Load your games first if you want to see the effect of a change here right away.

Don't have your own repertoire lines yet?

Pick a common opening below to use its standard main lines as a starting point. This is general, widely-known theory (not a specific course) at modest depth - a real starting point, not a substitute for deep study once you know what you're working on.


Optional: Import your own repertoire lines

Built-in matching only covers the courses already baked into this page. To check your games against your own repertoire instead, upload a small PGN where each "game" is one reference line, with the line's name in the Event tag - e.g. [Event "Chapter 3 | 7.Re1 Qc8"] followed by the moves. Most course/study tools can export something close to this, or you can type it by hand.

Everything you've saved, in this browser. Switch which one is active per slot, rename, or delete ones you don't need anymore.

Results

Note: centipawn-cost numbers aren't available here (that requires a chess engine, which this page doesn't run) - this shows deviation frequency and outcome correlation only.

Your Structures & Plans ?

Recurring opening structures found in your own games, auto-classified against 10 known pawn structures (IQP, Carlsbad, Hanging Pawns, Stonewall, Maroczy Bind/Hedgehog, Boleslavsky Hole, Double Iso, Doubled Pawns, Benoni/KID chains, and closed centers) - with the real middlegame plan and a few concrete checks filled in automatically, no theory required from you. If nothing matches, or the auto-detected plan doesn't fit what you're actually trying to do, you can always write your own instead. Saved in this browser so it's here next time.

What This Tool Actually Does

Opening courses and coaches tell you what you're supposed to play and why a plan works. What they can't easily tell you is whether any of that is actually showing up in your real games. This tool reads your games, compares them against your real course material move-by-move, and answers three concrete questions:

  • Where do you actually leave the book? Not "you should know theory" in the abstract - the exact move, in the exact line, that you keep deviating from.
  • Does that deviation cost you? Ranked by how often it happens and how often it correlates with a loss - so you're not just studying whatever line is fresh in your memory, you're studying what's actually hurting your results.
  • Are you executing the plan, not just the moves? Real opening theory is followed by a middlegame plan - a pawn break, a piece maneuver, a specific idea the position is asking for. This checks whether those specific plan elements actually show up in your games, not just whether you followed known theory.

Why This Actually Helps You Improve

The single biggest trap in opening study is confidently studying the wrong thing - drilling a line you already handle fine, while the actual leak in your results is somewhere you haven't looked closely at because it doesn't feel like the problem. This tool replaces that feeling with a real count: which lines you actually face, which deviations actually correlate with losses, and which plan elements are consistently missing when you lose. A pattern that shows up in 3 games might be noise. The same pattern holding up across 20-30 games is something worth restructuring your study around.

How To Use It

Start here, in this order: go to the Sync tab first. Sync your games from Chess.com/Lichess (or upload a PGN), then pick or upload the repertoire you actually play - either a starter opening from the dropdown, or your own imported lines. The White, Black vs 1.e4, and Black vs 1.d4 tabs only have something to show you once both of those are done - they're checking your games against your repertoire, so until you've told the page what that is, there's nothing to check.

Once you've synced and picked a repertoire, explore the tabs above:

  • White / Black vs 1.e4 / Black vs 1.d4 - each is a separate side/opening with its own findings: Study Priority (your highest-value lines to review, ranked by real cost), Middlegame Plans (whether you're executing the strategic idea, not just the opening moves), and Chapter Frequency (which parts of your repertoire actually come up).
  • Overview - what you actually play and face with both colors, even outside your chosen repertoire - useful for spotting a gap you haven't formally studied at all.
  • Game Explorer - every real deviation found, with a board view showing your move and the book's move as arrows.

On the Sync tab, you have a few ways to get games and a repertoire in:

  1. Sync directly from your Chess.com or Lichess username, or upload a PGN file you've exported.
  2. Pick a starter opening from the dropdown if you don't have your own repertoire file yet, or upload your own lines (a small PGN where each line is tagged with a name in the Event field).
  3. Optionally check "compute engine cost" to get real centipawn values for your top deviations - this runs a full chess engine right in your browser, so it takes a bit longer (pick a speed setting to control how long).
  4. Click "View" on any deviation to see the exact position on a board, with your move and the book's move shown as arrows.

Everything runs in your browser - your games, your analysis, and (if you use it) the chess engine itself. Nothing is uploaded to a server.

What To Study First

Ranked by risk score: score = total centipawns lost to deviations + (100 × deviations that happened in a game you lost) + (2 × how often you face this line). Lines you deviate on AND lose with float to the top.
